newsitem.title: SWEDEN: SSAB says sees steel demand improving.
newsitem.headline: SSAB says sees steel demand improving.

text.p: Swedish steel company SSAB said on Friday that it saw demand for steel gradually improving as it posted its results for the first six months of 1997.
SSAB reported a 27 percent fall in profit after financial items to 1.08 billion crowns which was in line with market expectations.
"We now see gradually better demand," chief executive Leif Gustafsson said in a statement, adding demand was expected to increase somewhat further during the rest of 1997.
"At the same time raw materials costs will rise as ore and coal deals give full cost effects in the second half of the year," SSAB said.
SSAB raised steel prices in Europe both in the second quarter and ahead of the third quarter. The latest price hike meant an increase of 3-4 percent in local currencies, it said.
Product prices will be the key factor for earnings development.
Six-month sales slipped three percent to 8.97 billion crowns, with lower prices having a negative impact of six percentate points and higher volumes boosting the figures by three percentage points.
Operating profit fell to 1.02 billion crowns from 1.31 billion in the corresponding year-earlier period while earnings per share fell to 5.90 from 8.30.
"Steel consumption picked up somewhat within the European Union (EU) in the first half of the year," SSAB said.
"At the same time capacity utilisation rose within the European steel industry and production was about seven percent higher than last year."

Market trends were stronger in the second quarter, lifting profit after financial items to 608 million crowns from 470 million crowns in the first quarter and close to the 642 million crowns posted in the second quarter of 1996.
